      "text": "Here are the structured, analytical notes based on the lecture transcript provided.\n\n***\n\n# Lecture Notes: Ionic Bonding, Metallic Solids, and Molecular Orbital Theory\n**Date:** [[2025-11-18]]\n**Topic:** [[Chemical Bonding]]\n**Lecturer:** (Context implies Chemistry Professor)\n**Tags:** #chemistry #bonding #physical-chemistry #quantum-mechanics #obsidian-notes\n\n---\n\n## 1. Ionic Bonding and Lattice Energy\n### 1.1 The Nature of the Ionic Bond\nIonic bonding is fundamentally different from covalent bonding. It is **nondirectional** and based purely on **electrostatic attraction** between ions of opposite charges.\n\n*   **Formation:** Element A gives an electron to Element B $\\rightarrow$ Cation ($A^+$) + Anion ($B^-$).\n*   **Geometry:** Spherical symmetry of the field (Coulombic). The ions pack to maximize attraction and minimize repulsion.\n\n### 1.2 Electrostatic Interaction (Coulomb\u0027s Law)\nThe force ($F$) and Potential Energy ($E$) between two ions define the bond strength.\n\n$$ E_{el} \\propto \\frac{Q^+ Q^-}{d} $$\n\nWhere:\n*   $Q^+, Q^-$ \u003d charges of the ions.\n*   $d$ \u003d distance between the centers of the nuclei.\n\n**Critical Analysis of Bond Strength:**\n1.  **Charge Magnitude:** The greater the charge, the stronger the attraction.\n    *   *Example:* $MgO$ ($Mg^{2+}O^{2-}$) has much stronger attraction than $NaCl$ ($Na^+Cl^-$).\n2.  **Interionic Distance:** The smaller the ions (shorter $d$), the stronger the attraction.\n    *   *Comparison:* $LiF$ vs. $CsI$. Lithium and Fluorine are smaller $\\rightarrow$ stronger bond $\\rightarrow$ higher melting point.\n\n### 1.3 Ionic Radii Trends\n*   **Cations:** Always *smaller* than their parent atom (loss of valence shell, effective nuclear charge $Z_{eff}$ pulls remaining electrons closer).\n*   **Anions:** Always *larger* than their parent atom (electron-electron repulsion expands the cloud).\n\n\u003e [!NOTE] Critical Insight: Isoelectronic Series\n\u003e When comparing ions with the same number of electrons (e.g., $Na^+, F^-, Mg^{2+}$), the size is determined solely by the number of protons. More protons $\\rightarrow$ higher $Z_{eff}$ $\\rightarrow$ smaller radius.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Ionic Crystal Structures \u0026 Coordination\nThe structure of an ionic solid is determined by the **ratio of ionic radii** ($r_{cation} / r_{anion}$). This dictates how many anions can pack around a cation (Coordination Number - CN).\n\n### 2.1 Coordination Number (CN)\nThe number of nearest neighbors of opposite charge.\n\n| Structure Type | Coordination (Cat:An) | Packing Geometry | Example |\n| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |\n| **[[Zinc Blende]] (ZnS)** | 4:4 | Tetrahedral holes | $ZnS$, $CuCl$ |\n| **[[Rock Salt]] (NaCl)** | 6:6 | Octahedral holes | $NaCl$, $MgO$ |\n| **[[Cesium Chloride]] (CsCl)** | 8:8 | Cubic holes | $CsCl$ |\n\n### 2.2 Analyzing the Structures\n1.  **NaCl (6:6):**\n    *   Standard face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice of anions with cations in octahedral holes.\n    *   Valid for medium-sized cations relative to anions.\n    *   SMILES (approx): `[Na+].[Cl-]` (infinite lattice)\n2.  **CsCl (8:8):**\n    *   Cation is very large (Cs is in period 6). It pushes anions further apart, allowing 8 neighbors.\n    *   *Not* BCC (Body Centered Cubic) in the atomic sense, but a simple cubic lattice of anions with a cation in the center.\n3.  **ZnS (4:4):**\n    *   Cation is small. Fits into tetrahedral holes.\n\n\u003e [!WARNING] Analysis of Coordination Geometry\n\u003e Do not confuse the unit cell shape with coordination geometry. A cubic unit cell can contain tetrahedral coordination sites (like in ZnS). The coordination number is strictly a count of *immediate* neighbors.\n\n### 2.3 Lattice Energy\nThe energy released when gaseous ions form a solid crystal lattice (Exothermic).\n$$ M_{(g)}^+ + X_{(g)}^- \\rightarrow MX_{(s)} \\quad \\Delta H_{latt} \u003c 0 $$\n\n**Trends:**\n*   $\\uparrow$ Charge \u003d $\\uparrow \\uparrow$ Lattice Energy.\n*   $\\downarrow$ Size \u003d $\\uparrow$ Lattice Energy.\n*   **Consequence:** High lattice energy implies high melting point, hardness, and brittleness.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Metallic Bonding\n### 3.1 The Electron Sea Model\n*   **Structure:** Metal cations arranged in a crystal lattice.\n*   **Electrons:** Valence electrons are **delocalized** over the entire crystal (not bound to a specific atom).\n*   **Result:** \"Sea of electrons\" holding the cations together via electrostatic attraction.\n\n### 3.2 Properties Derived from Model\n1.  **Electrical Conductivity:** Electrons are free to move (charge carriers).\n2.  **Thermal Conductivity:** Free electrons transfer kinetic energy rapidly.\n3.  **Malleability/Ductility:** The bond is non-directional. Atoms can slide past each other without breaking the \"sea\" attraction (unlike ionic crystals which shatter due to like-charge repulsion upon shifting).\n\n---\n\n## 4. Covalent Bonding Theories\nWe moved from simple models to quantum mechanical descriptions.\n\n### 4.1 Valence Bond (VB) Theory (Review)\n*   **Concept:** Overlap of atomic orbitals.\n*   **Localization:** Electrons are localized between two atoms.\n*   **Pro:** Great for molecular geometry ([[Hybridization]]).\n*   **Con:** Fails to explain magnetic properties (e.g., Paramagnetism of $O_2$) and excited states.\n\n### 4.2 [[Molecular Orbital Theory]] (MO Theory)\n*   **Concept:** Atomic orbitals (AO) from *all* atoms in a molecule combine to form Molecular Orbitals (MO).\n*   **Delocalization:** Electrons belong to the whole molecule.\n*   **Method:** Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO).\n\n---\n\n## 5. Molecular Orbital Theory: Critical Analysis\n\n### 5.1 LCAO Principles\nWhen two atomic wave functions ($\\psi_A$ and $\\psi_B$) combine:\n\n1.  **Constructive Interference ($\\psi_A + \\psi_B$):**\n    *   Increases electron density *between* nuclei.\n    *   **Bonding MO** ($\\sigma, \\pi$).\n    *   Energy is **lower** than original atomic orbitals.\n2.  **Destructive Interference ($\\psi_A - \\psi_B$):**\n    *   Cancels electron density between nuclei (creates a **Node**).\n    *   **Antibonding MO** ($\\sigma^*, \\pi^*$).\n    *   Energy is **higher** than original atomic orbitals.\n\n\u003e [!NOTE] Conservation of Orbitals\n\u003e The number of MOs formed *must* equal the number of AOs combined.\n\u003e 2 Atomic Orbitals $\\rightarrow$ 1 Bonding MO + 1 Antibonding MO.\n\n### 5.2 Sigma ($\\sigma$) vs. Pi ($\\pi$) Overlap\n*   **Sigma ($\\sigma$):** Head-on overlap. Cylindrically symmetric along the internuclear axis. (e.g., $s-s$, $p_z-p_z$).\n*   **Pi ($\\pi$):** Sideways overlap. Electron density above and below the axis. Node along the axis. (e.g., $p_x-p_x$, $p_y-p_y$).\n\n### 5.3 The Period 2 Diatomic Anomaly (Warning!)\nFor homonuclear diatomics ($X_2$):\nThere is a distinct crossover in energy levels between $N_2$ and $O_2$.\n\n**Group 1 ($B_2, C_2, N_2$):**\nThere is significant $s-p$ mixing because the $2s$ and $2p$ energy gap is small.\n*   **Result:** The $\\sigma_{2p}$ orbital is pushed *higher* in energy than the $\\pi_{2p}$ orbitals.\n*   **Ordering:** $\\sigma_{2s} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2s} \u003c \\pi_{2p} \u003c \\sigma_{2p} \u003c \\pi^*_{2p} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2p}$\n\n**Group 2 ($O_2, F_2$):**\nThe $2s-2p$ energy gap is large (due to higher $Z_{eff}$). Mixing is negligible.\n*   **Result:** The \"normal\" expected ordering.\n*   **Ordering:** $\\sigma_{2s} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2s} \u003c \\sigma_{2p} \u003c \\pi_{2p} \u003c \\pi^*_{2p} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2p}$\n\n\u003e [!WARNING] Exam Trap\n\u003e When drawing the MO diagram for $N_2$, remember that the $\\pi$ bond is lower energy than the $\\sigma$ bond. For $O_2$, the $\\sigma$ drops below the $\\pi$. This changes the magnetic properties and bond orders!\n\n### 5.4 Bond Order Formula\n$$ \\text{Bond Order} \u003d \\frac{1}{2} (N_{bonding} - N_{antibonding}) $$\n*   BO \u003d 1: Single bond.\n*   BO \u003d 2: Double bond.\n*   BO \u003d 0: Molecule does not exist (e.g., $He_2$).\n\n### 5.5 Magnetic Properties\n*   **Diamagnetic:** All electrons paired. Repelled by magnetic fields. (e.g., $N_2$).\n*   **Paramagnetic:** At least one unpaired electron. Attracted to magnetic fields.\n    *   **Proof of MO Theory:** Lewis structure of $O_2$ predicts paired electrons (double bond). MO theory correctly predicts **two unpaired electrons** in the $\\pi^*_{2p}$ orbitals. This explains why liquid oxygen is magnetic.\n\n---\n\n## 6. General Formulas \u0026 Identities Used\n\n*   **Coulomb\u0027s Law:** $F \u003d k \\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$\n*   **Bond Order:** $BO \u003d 0.5(N_b - N_a)$\n*   **Formal Charge:** $FC \u003d V - N - \\frac{B}{2}$ (Valence - Nonbonding - Bonding/2)\n\n---\n\n## 7. Contextual \u0026 Memorialization Notes\n*   **Lecture Flow:** The professor used the visual of magnets/poles to explain the paramagnetism of liquid oxygen—specifically mentioning pouring liquid oxygen between magnet poles.\n*   **Visuals:** Much time was spent distinguishing the shapes of the \"lobes\" in p-orbitals and how the signs (+/-) of the wave function determine bonding vs. antibonding.\n*   **Emphasis:** Strong emphasis on why ionic crystals shatter (brittleness) compared to metals (malleability) due to the alignment of charges.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Wikilinks for Expansion\n*   [[Born-Haber Cycle]] (For precise lattice energy calculation)\n*   [[Band Theory]] (Expansion of MO theory for infinite metallic lattices)\n*   [[Hybridization]] (Connection back to Valence Bond Theory)\n*   [[Photoelectron Spectroscopy]] (Experimental evidence for orbital energies)",

      }, {
        "text": "Delta H_{latt} \u003c 0 $$\n\n**Trends:**\n*   $\\uparrow$ Charge \u003d $\\uparrow \\"
      }, {
        "text": "uparrow$ Lattice Energy.\n*   $\\downarrow$ Size \u003d $\\uparrow$ Lattice Energy.\n*   **Consequence"
      }, {
        "text": ":** High lattice energy implies high melting point, hardness, and brittleness.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Metallic Bonding\n###"
      }, {
        "text": " 3.1 The Electron Sea Model\n*   **Structure:** Metal cations arranged in a crystal lattice.\n*   **Electrons"
      }, {
        "text": ":** Valence electrons are **delocalized** over the entire crystal (not bound to a specific atom).\n*   **Result"
      }, {
        "text": ":** \"Sea of electrons\" holding the cations together via electrostatic attraction.\n\n### 3.2 Properties Derived from Model\n1.  **Electrical"
      }, {
        "text": " Conductivity:** Electrons are free to move (charge carriers).\n2.  **Thermal Conductivity:** Free electrons transfer kinetic energy rapidly"
      }, {
        "text": ".\n3.  **Malleability/Ductility:** The bond is non-directional. Atoms can slide"
      }, {
        "text": " past each other without breaking the \"sea\" attraction (unlike ionic crystals which shatter due to like-charge repulsion upon shifting"
      }, {
        "text": ").\n\n---\n\n## 4. Covalent Bonding Theories\nWe moved from simple models to quantum mechanical descriptions.\n\n### 4.1 Valence"
      }, {
        "text": " Bond (VB) Theory (Review)\n*   **Concept:** Overlap of atomic orbitals.\n*   **Localization:**"
      }, {
        "text": " Electrons are localized between two atoms.\n*   **Pro:** Great for molecular geometry ([[Hybridization]]).\n*   **Con"
      }, {
        "text": ":** Fails to explain magnetic properties (e.g., Paramagnetism of $O_2$) and excited states.\n\n### 4.2"
      }, {
        "text": " [[Molecular Orbital Theory]] (MO Theory)\n*   **Concept:** Atomic orbitals (AO) from *all* atoms in a molecule combine to"
      }, {
        "text": " form Molecular Orbitals (MO).\n*   **Delocalization:** Electrons belong to the whole molecule.\n*   **Method"
      }, {
        "text": ":** Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO).\n\n---\n\n## 5. Molecular Orbital Theory: Critical Analysis\n\n"
      }, {
        "text": "### 5.1 LCAO Principles\nWhen two atomic wave functions ($\\psi_A$ and $\\psi_B$) combine:\n\n"
      }, {
        "text": "1.  **Constructive Interference ($\\psi_A + \\psi_B$):**\n    *   Incre"
      }, {
        "text": "ases electron density *between* nuclei.\n    *   **Bonding MO** ($\\sigma, \\pi$).\n    *   Energy"
      }, {
        "text": " is **lower** than original atomic orbitals.\n2.  **Destructive Interference ($\\psi_A - \\psi_B$):**\n    "
      }, {
        "text": "*   Cancels electron density between nuclei (creates a **Node**).\n    *   **Antibonding MO** ($\\sigma"
      }, {
        "text": "^*, \\pi^*$).\n    *   Energy is **higher** than original atomic orbitals.\n\n\u003e [!"
      }, {
        "text": "NOTE] Conservation of Orbitals\n\u003e The number of MOs formed *must* equal the number of AOs combined.\n\u003e "
      }, {
        "text": "2 Atomic Orbitals $\\rightarrow$ 1 Bonding MO + 1 Antibonding MO.\n\n### 5.2 Sigma"
      }, {
        "text": " ($\\sigma$) vs. Pi ($\\pi$) Overlap\n*   **Sigma ($\\sigma$):** Head-on overlap."
      }, {
        "text": " Cylindrically symmetric along the internuclear axis. (e.g., $s-s$, $p_z-p_z$)."
      }, {
        "text": "\n*   **Pi ($\\pi$):** Sideways overlap. Electron density above and below the axis. Node along"
      }, {
        "text": " the axis. (e.g., $p_x-p_x$, $p_y-p_"
      }, {
        "text": "y$).\n\n### 5.3 The Period 2 Diatomic Anomaly (Warning!)\nFor homonuclear diatomics ($X"
      }, {
        "text": "_2$):\nThere is a distinct crossover in energy levels between $N_2$ and $O_2$.\n\n**Group"
      }, {
        "text": " 1 ($B_2, C_2, N_2$):**\nThere is significant $s-p$ mixing"
      }, {
        "text": " because the $2s$ and $2p$ energy gap is small.\n*   **Result:** The $\\sigma_{2p}$ orbital is"
      }, {
        "text": " pushed *higher* in energy than the $\\pi_{2p}$ orbitals.\n*   **Ordering:** $\\sigma"
      }, {
        "text": "_{2s} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2s} \u003c \\pi_{2p} \u003c \\sigma_{2p"
      }, {
        "text": "} \u003c \\pi^*_{2p} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2p}$\n\n**Group 2 ($O_2"
      }, {
        "text": ", F_2$):**\nThe $2s-2p$ energy gap is large (due to higher"
      }, {
        "text": " $Z_{eff}$). Mixing is negligible.\n*   **Result:** The \"normal\" expected ordering.\n*   **Ordering:** $\\sigma"
      }, {
        "text": "_{2s} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2s} \u003c \\sigma_{2p} \u003c \\pi_{2p} \u003c \\pi^*_{2"

        "text": "p} \u003c \\sigma^*_{2p}$\n\n\u003e [!WARNING] Exam Trap\n\u003e When drawing the MO diagram for $N_2$,"
      }, {
        "text": " remember that the $\\pi$ bond is lower energy than the $\\sigma$ bond. For $O_2$, the $\\sigma"

        "text": "$ drops below the $\\pi$. This changes the magnetic properties and bond orders!\n\n### 5.4 Bond Order"
      }, {
        "text": " Formula\n$$ \\text{Bond Order} \u003d \\frac{1}{2} (N_{bonding} - N_{"

        "text": "antibonding}) $$\n*   BO \u003d 1: Single bond.\n*   BO \u003d 2: Double bond.\n*   "

      "text": "Here is the expanded, dedicated note for the **[[Born-Haber Cycle]]**.\n\nThis note connects directly to the **Lattice Energy** section of the previous lecture. It provides the thermodynamic justification for the bond strengths discussed earlier.\n\n***\n\n# Note: Born-Haber Cycle\n**Parent Topic:** [[Chemical Bonding]]\n**Related Topics:** [[Thermodynamics]], [[Hess\u0027s Law]], [[Lattice Energy]], [[Ionization Energy]]\n**Tags:** #thermodynamics #physical-chemistry #derivation #cycle\n\n---\n\n## 1. Conceptual Foundation\nThe **Born-Haber Cycle** is a thermodynamic cycle that applies **[[Hess\u0027s Law]]** to ionic solids. Since **Lattice Energy ($\\Delta H_{latt}$)** cannot be measured directly in a laboratory, we calculate it indirectly by constructing a closed loop of measurable thermodynamic steps.\n\n### The Core Principle (Hess\u0027s Law)\nThe change in enthalpy ($\\Delta H$) is independent of the pathway.\n1.  **Direct Path:** Forming the solid directly from elements in their standard states ($\\Delta H^\\circ_f$).\n2.  **Indirect Path:** Turning elements into gas $\\rightarrow$ creating ions $\\rightarrow$ combining ions to form the lattice.\n\nSince state functions are path-independent:\n$$ \\Delta H (\\text{Direct}) \u003d \\sum \\Delta H (\\text{Indirect Steps}) $$\n\n---\n\n## 2. Step-by-Step Derivation (The Indirect Path)\n\nLet us construct the cycle for a generic metal halide $MX_{(s)}$ (e.g., $NaCl$).\n\n### Step 1: Sublimation / Atomization of Metal\nWe must convert the solid metal into individual gaseous atoms.\n*   **Process:** $M_{(s)} \\rightarrow M_{(g)}$\n*   **Energy:** Enthalpy of Sublimation ($\\Delta H_{sub}$) or Atomization ($\\Delta H_{at}$).\n*   **Sign:** **Endothermic (+)** (Requires energy to break metallic bonds).\n\n### Step 2: Dissociation of Non-Metal\nWe must create individual gaseous atoms from the diatomic non-metal molecule.\n*   **Process:** $\\frac{1}{2} X_{2(g)} \\rightarrow X_{(g)}$\n*   **Energy:** Bond Dissociation Energy ($D$) or Enthalpy of Atomization.\n*   **Formula:** $\\Delta H_{at} \u003d \\frac{1}{2} D_{X-X}$\n*   **Sign:** **Endothermic (+)** (Requires energy to break the covalent bond).\n\n\u003e [!WARNING] Stoichiometry Trap\n\u003e Pay close attention to the coefficients. If you are forming $NaCl$, you need **one** Cl atom, so you use $\\frac{1}{2}$ of the bond energy of $Cl_2$. If you are forming $MgCl_2$, you need **two** Cl atoms, so you use the full bond energy of $Cl_2$ ($1 \\times D_{Cl-Cl}$).\n\n### Step 3: Ionization of Metal (Cation Formation)\nRemove electrons from the gaseous metal atom.\n*   **Process:** $M_{(g)} \\rightarrow M^+_{(g)} + e^-$\n*   **Energy:** Ionization Energy ($IE$).\n*   **Sign:** **Endothermic (+)** (Requires energy to overcome nuclear attraction).\n*   *Note:* If forming $Mg^{2+}$, you must add the first ($IE_1$) AND second ($IE_2$) ionization energies.\n\n### Step 4: Electron Affinity (Anion Formation)\nAdd electrons to the gaseous non-metal atom.\n*   **Process:** $X_{(g)} + e^- \\rightarrow X^-_{(g)}$\n*   **Energy:** Electron Affinity ($EA$).\n*   **Sign:** **Exothermic (-)** for the *first* EA (energy is released when a neutral atom gains an electron).\n*   *Critical Note:* The **2nd Electron Affinity** (e.g., forming $O^{2-}$ from $O^-$) is always **Endothermic (+)** due to repulsion between the negative electron and the negative ion.\n\n### Step 5: Lattice Formation\nGaseous ions combine to form the solid crystal lattice.\n*   **Process:** $M^+_{(g)} + X^-_{(g)} \\rightarrow MX_{(s)}$\n*   **Energy:** Lattice Enthalpy ($\\Delta H_{latt}$).\n*   **Sign:** **Highly Exothermic (-)** (Formation of strong electrostatic bonds).\n\n---\n\n## 3. The Master Equation\n\nBy equating the Direct Path ($\\Delta H^\\circ_f$) with the sum of the Indirect Path steps:\n\n$$ \\Delta H^\\circ_f \u003d \\Delta H_{sub} + \\Delta H_{diss} + IE + EA + \\Delta H_{latt} $$\n\nTo find the Lattice Energy (the unknown), we rearrange:\n\n$$ \\Delta H_{latt} \u003d \\Delta H^\\circ_f - (\\Delta H_{sub} + \\Delta H_{diss} + IE + EA) $$\n\n### Example: Sodium Chloride (NaCl)\nUsing standard values (in $kJ/mol$):\n\n1.  $\\Delta H^\\circ_f [NaCl]$: $-411$ (Total energy of formation)\n2.  $\\Delta H_{sub} [Na]$: $+107$\n3.  $\\frac{1}{2} D_{Cl-Cl}$: $+122$\n4.  $IE_1 [Na]$: $+496$\n5.  $EA_1 [Cl]$: $-349$\n\n**Calculation:**\n$$ -411 \u003d (+107) + (+122) + (+496) + (-349) + \\Delta H_{latt} $$\n$$ -411 \u003d 376 + \\Delta H_{latt} $$\n$$ \\Delta H_{latt} \u003d -411 - 376 $$\n$$ \\Delta H_{latt} \u003d -787 \\; kJ/mol $$\n\n\u003e [!NOTE] Result Analysis\n\u003e The result is negative, indicating that the formation of the lattice releases a massive amount of energy. This is the \"payoff\" that drives the reaction, compensating for the energy \"costs\" of sublimation, dissociation, and ionization.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Critical Analysis: Definition of Lattice Energy\n\nThere is a frequent ambiguity in textbooks regarding the sign of $\\Delta H_{latt}$.\n\n1.  **Lattice Formation Enthalpy:** $M^+_{(g)} + X^-_{(g)} \\rightarrow MX_{(s)}$. This is **Exothermic (-)**. (Used in the derivation above).\n2.  **Lattice Dissociation Enthalpy:** $MX_{(s)} \\rightarrow M^+_{(g)} + X^-_{(g)}$. This is **Endothermic (+)**.\n\n**Warning:** Always check the definition provided in the problem statement. The magnitude is the same ($787 kJ/mol$), only the sign changes. If the question asks for \"Lattice Energy\" as a positive value, they represent the energy required to *break* the lattice.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Application: Why doesn\u0027t $NaCl_2$ exist?\nWe can use the Born-Haber cycle to prove why hypothetical compounds are unstable.\n\n**Hypothesis:** Why not $Na^{2+} (Cl^-)_2$?\n*   **Benefit:** The Lattice Energy ($\\Delta H_{latt}$) for a $+2$ ion ($Na^{2+}$) would be roughly $3\\times$ to $4\\times$ larger than for $NaCl$. This is a huge exothermic contribution.\n*   **Cost:** To get $Na^{2+}$, we need the **Second Ionization Energy ($IE_2$)** of Sodium.\n    *   $Na$ configuration: $[Ne]3s^1$.\n    *   Removing the 2nd electron breaks the stable noble gas core $[Ne]$.\n    *   $IE_2$ for Na is massive (~$4560 \\; kJ/mol$).\n\n**Conclusion:** The increase in Lattice Energy (payoff) is **not enough** to compensate for the massive energy cost ($IE_2$) of breaking the noble gas core. Therefore, $\\Delta H^\\circ_f$ would be highly positive (endothermic), making $NaCl_2$ unstable.\n\n---\n\n## 6. General Formulas\n*   **Hess\u0027s Law Loop:** $\\sum \\Delta H_{\\text{clockwise}} \u003d \\sum \\Delta H_{\\text{counter-clockwise}}$\n*   **Lattice Energy (Kapustinskii Equation approximation):**\n    $$ U_L \\approx \\frac{K \\cdot \\nu \\cdot |z^+| \\cdot |z^-|}{r^+ + r^-} \\left( 1 - \\frac{d}{r^+ + r^-} \\right) $$\n    *(Used when experimental Born-Haber data is missing; connects back to ionic radii).*\n\n---\n**WikiLinks:**\n*   [[Hess\u0027s Law]]\n*   [[Entropy and Spontaneity]] (Why exothermic reactions aren\u0027t always spontaneous)\n*   [[Kapustinskii Equation]]",
